subsubtopic: PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT CENTRE
speechtext:
1.	Did the Task Force Report of December 15, 1972 in connection with the requirements for a Pacific Environment Centre (TEAG) state that employees and the public will have difficulty with access to this site and, if so (a) what plans have been made to overcome this problem (b) do the estimates for the Environment Centre include additional costs which will be required to meet this problem?
2.	Did the Report indicate that a Third Crossing of Burrard Inlet may be necessary, particularly with respect to location of site facilities and, if so, what has been the reaction of the Vancouver City Council and the Government of British Columbia to such a proposal?
3.	Did the Report indicate that by the time the Centre is ready for occupancy in 1976 or 1977 there will be over 400 persons employed at the proposed new site and, if so, has the government
July 25, 1973

taken into consideration (a) the environmental impact (b) the traffic congestion (c) the additional air pollution which may be generated on this route and in the area of the proposed site?

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT CENTRE
speechtext:
1. The TEAG Report recognized that the proposed site will cause a major change in commuting patterns for many employees. The Report suggested the need for over-or-under crossing of the railroad tracks and for at least two access/egress roads to the site. TEAG is being re-engaged to report further on solutions to these problems.
2.	The third crossing was being actively considered by all three levels of government at the time of the TEAG study. The TEAG Report indicated that the possibility of a crossing of Burrard Inlet being built near the site may prove a significant factor in site planning. An in-depth study of the matter will be needed before final decisions are made regarding location of site facilities. There has been little evidence since that time that the three levels of government will proceed with a third crossing in the near future.
3.	The TEAG Report estimated 446 employees on the site by the end of 1977; (a) the Centre will enhance the immediate environment and is planned as a stimulating working milieu for employees and an attractive information centre for visitors: (b) TEAG is being re-engaged to provide a further study of traffic problems; and (c) it is the intention that the Centre will set a good example by strictly observing existing criteria and regulations designed to preserve air quality. It is planned to accommodate a tower, equipped with air quality sensors, at the Centre.

subtopic: TAPS TANKER ROUTE-AMOUNT OF OIL TO BE SHIPPED TO CHERRY POINT REFINERY-POSSIBLE CANADIAN COMMITMENT OF SUPPLIES AS ALTERNATIVE

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TAPS TANKER ROUTE-AMOUNT OF OIL TO BE SHIPPED TO CHERRY POINT REFINERY-POSSIBLE CANADIAN COMMITMENT OF SUPPLIES AS ALTERNATIVE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. Inasmuch as the Acting Prime Minister now considers the TAPS line and the associated tanker system no longer simply hypothetical matters, can he tell the House what information this government has acquired from the government of the United States as to how much Alaskan oil in terms of barrels per day or barrels per week will be moved through the Straits of Juan de Fuca?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TAPS TANKER ROUTE-AMOUNT OF OIL TO BE SHIPPED TO CHERRY POINT REFINERY-POSSIBLE CANADIAN COMMITMENT OF SUPPLIES AS ALTERNATIVE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not have before me now the quantities, but I think it is relative to the position we have been establishing with the United States administration that it is only a very small proportion of the oil that will be moving from Alaska to the mainland United States. I have heard figures of around 10 per cent, so that if the tankers were to bypass Juan de Fuca, as we would like them to, it would not have any over-all effect of any significance for the project which could proceed without any damage or danger to the Canadian environment.

subtopic: TAPS TANKER ROUTE-AMOUNT OF OIL TO BE SHIPPED TO CHERRY POINT REFINERY-POSSIBLE CANADIAN COMMITMENT OF SUPPLIES AS ALTERNATIVE
speechtext: A supplementary question. What moves does the Secretary of State for External Affairs intend to take to get some firm information on this? I presume, since he is talking about only starting to fight, he intends to offer some unambiguous and possibly attractive alternatives to the Americans in this connection. In relation to supplies of crude for American refineries in the Puget Sound area, what is the Canadian government offering by way of firm guarantees with regard to deliveries of Canadian crude overland to those refineries as an alternative to them being supplied by sea through the Straits of Juan de Fuca? Has the government of Canada made a firm commitment and if so, for how much?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TAPS TANKER ROUTE-AMOUNT OF OIL TO BE SHIPPED TO CHERRY POINT REFINERY-POSSIBLE CANADIAN COMMITMENT OF SUPPLIES AS ALTERNATIVE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is we have not yet done that. I think it would be logical that if we were to expect that this refinery is to be supplied from inland rather than from tankers entering the narrow waters of the Straits of Juan de Fuca, that we would have to enter into some agreements with the United States that would not expose that refinery to the possibility of being unable to operate.

as an alternative to this oil coming in through the Straits of Juan de Fuca? Has any study been definitely commissioned to date?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill was given considerable attention in committee, both by members of the standing committee and by other interested members of the House. As an observer at the committee meetings, I am of the opinion that a great disservice will be done to the Canadian people by passing this legislation.
I am not at all sure of the ramifications of the lottery or of the postage issues. I am inclined to believe the public will show considerable interest in buying postage stamps, costing an additional two cents, for mail to be sent from the Olympic site during the Olympic games in 1976. However, I view with great reluctance the provision in the bill with regard to coinage.
July 25, 1973

It is proposed that a major part of the financing of the games be undertaken by issuing a new type of coinage in denominations of $5 and $10. These will be packaged in a number of ways. There will be proof sets, souvenir package sets and sets containing all the additional silver coin denominations. The market for coinage and commemorative monetary tokens have grown over the years, particularly during the last ten years, to the extent that many organizations use the minting of coinage and medallions to assist in financing their operations. This has been particularly true in Canada since 1967 when most cities across this country put out a medallion-which may or may not have contained silver-to commemorate, in effect, a particular event in their area. There is no question that this market has grown and in Canada we now have two or three mints producing medallions.
It is also true, Mr. Speaker, that in the minting of coinage Canada has been able to expand its operation to a considerable degree. Only a few years ago we were asking the United States government to mint our ten-cent coins because we did not have the capacity to do so. I am pleased to see that the Mint has been expanded and has achieved a degree of expertise in the development of coinage so that we are now producing silver and metal currency for 20 countries. This is a credit to the Canadian Mint and to our ability to meet the growing need for currency.
With regard to developing coins in Canada, I am told that since confederation we have minted in total $317 million. Mr. Speaker, $317 million in silver currency is not a very large amount, but it has been sufficient to meet our needs for the past 100 years. Now we are being asked by Mayor Drapeau and by COJO to allow the minting of approximately $450 million of new currency. This is not a medallion but a piece of currency that can be used in trade by Canadians, that is legal tender and can be used in financial transactions within our country. It is, in fact, the issuing of more coinage currency than we have used in this country for the past 100 years.
Mr. Speaker, for hundreds of years medallions have been issued to commemorate the holding of the Olympic games. Only relatively recently countries have asked for the production of tenderable currency that could be used for the promotion of the Olympic games. In Canada in the past ten years, we have experienced with the development of commemorative coins and these have received considerable support from the public and Canadian coin collectors. A limited number have been bought by coin dealers in other countries as well.
It is interesting to note that little has been said about the fact that most countries prohibit the importation of another country's coinage. It is interesting to note, too, that in 1967, when for the first time in many years we included in our centennial sets a $20 gold piece, this coin could not legally be purchased even by numismatic organizations in the United States. The United States had laws that prevented its importation, therefore, coin dealers in that country were prohibited from buying our centennial sets containing the $20 gold piece.
Mr. Speaker, during the year that we celebrated our one hundredth birthday we had as large a market as we have
Olympic Bill
ever had for coin sets produced in Canada. During that period we produced and sold to the buying public in Canada and across the world slightly less than three million commemorative coins. This involved the $1 coin, the coin sets that ranged from a penny to $1 and the special presentation sets. The latter included the coin in which I am very proud to have played a considerable role leading to its production by persuading, over the years, three different finance ministers to allow it to be minted. I refer to the $20 gold coin that became the highlight of the coinage presentation sets put out in 1967.
In 1967, Mr. Speaker, we sold slightly less than three million sets. Now we are being asked by COJO to put out in stages legal tender to the extent of 65 million coins. To me this means that unless everybody in this country decides to keep coinage there will not be the number of collections that will dispose of 65 millions pieces. In effect, this would mean, if we were to sell the currency within this country, that every man, woman and child would end up with at least $20 worth of commemorative coinage to make up the $450 million issued. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that many people in this country have little interest in carrying around $5 or $10 silver pieces. Anyone who has studied this situation is aware that there is no possibility of our putting out $450 million worth of commemorative coinage and having it bought by collectors. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, how do we expect to dispose of it?
I listened to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) indicate that consideration had been given to methods of disposing of the coinage. We are aware that in this bill we are establishing an account for the Olympics committee that will allow the minting of this coinage in batches, starting in 1974, and that this account will be debited and credited, as the case may be, for the coinage that is bought. This is almost the system that was used in Germany. In the heat of national pride, the West German government decided to mint and print a very large commemorative issue. Most of this issue was handled through the German banks. Mr. Speaker, almost 50 per cent of that coinage is still sitting in the banks that bought it for national reasons, and they are now asking the government to buy it back.
It costs approximately 30 cents to make a $5 or $10 silver coin. These are not necessarily what they call proof sets, but are proof-like coinage. As I understand it, a proof set is struck with special dyes and is struck for a second time to give it a very clear image. The coinage we are speaking about will not be proof coinage but will be proof-like. It will be in a container. What will happen? Pressure will be applied in Montreal, where they are not above blackmailing the people of Canada, the federal government and even their own people. I am sure that at the height of their enthusiasm the authorities there will exhort the companies, various offices and entities such as our national banks to buy, buy, buy and, hopefully, dispose of the coins at a later date.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they have blackmailed us a number of times. I can think of two instances. The mayor of Montreal blackmailed us in the matter of the War Measures Act, and he blackmailed us into the centennial celebrations for which this parliament picked up much of the tab. Nobody objected particularly. Perhaps I should not use the word "blackmail" but I leave that connotation. I define blackmail as the use of strong methods to persuade people, perhaps for many good reasons, to do things they do not want to do. They do those things because they fear the consequences of not doing them.
I would not be surprised if the workers in Montreal go home with coinage in their pay packets as part payment for their work. They can take the coins out of the plastic wrapper and use them, or take them to the banks and get dollar bills for them. This will happen: it will have to happen, for the Olympic committee wants to raise something like $200 million. I suggest that the government will be less than honest with the country if it does not retain control of the minting of the coinage. The coinage should be sold and should not be dealt with as if one is operating a concession. It should be pruchased.
In 1967 the Mint struck centennial coinage. You sent in your order with the money, the Mint accepted the order and filled it later. It limited the number of coins which could be issued to one individual. Each package of coins had a face value of $1.91 but was sold for $3. Obviously, if too many packages were sold they would lose their value as collectors' pieces, so sales were retricted. The collector paid $3 for coins with a face value of $1.91, and the seigniorage on each sale was approximately $1.09. That nice profit accrued to the Canadian Mint. The Mint was reaslistic in issuing those coins. If you are asking $3 for $1.91 worth of coins, the coins must be collectors' items. If they are not collectors' items worth more than the face value of the coins, why would anybody be idiot enough to pay $3 for $1.91 worth of coins?

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext: A Liberal might be.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) BILL PROVISION FOR ISSUING OF COMMEMORATIVE COINS AND STAMPS AND HOLDING OF LOTTERY
speechtext:
The Liberals might do that. They seem to have adopted Social Credit ideas in this particular piece of legislation, because they are almost going to make money out of thin air. Obviously, if the Mint had said that it would issue more than so many sets of proof-like coin, each package of coins would have been worth $1.91 and not $3. Therefore, only by making such coins scarce could they be valuable as collectors' items.
That will not happen with the Olympic coins. We are talking about putting out coins that will be worth just about what you pay for them. Presumably, you could take them to the grocery store and spend them. As well, we are prepared under this program to put out more coinage than we have put out in our history as a nation, and we will do this in a period of two years.
The Americans steal our coins and melt them down. They make a profit on our coins because a number of them are made of silver. I remember when the little five-cent piece was worth more than ten cents on the silver market. Melted down, it was 90 per cent pure silver which was worth more than ten cents on the silver market. The Americans have been melting down our coins during the last six months. We have put out debased coinage to

prevent a considerable capital loss occurring to this country through the carrying away and melting down of our silver coins.
Apparently it will cost $2 to produce a $5 coin. The seigniorage on that sale will be about $3, less the 30 cents cost involved in the manufacture of each coin. Therefore, the seigniorage on each coin will be greater than the basic cost of the coin. One might call that the basic value. If silver does what gold has done in the last year, the advantage in the long run will accrue to the government. On the other hand, it may accrue io the collectors, or even to the United States government which seems to be smarter in this field than we are.
Why do I say that? If silver prices double, it may be more advantageous to melt down our new coins and turn them into silver bullion. Of course, I am speculating. The fact is that if we are putting out this amount of currency, the minting of it should be under the control of the government, of the Minister of Finance. It should not be under the control of an agency which will not sell the coins as currency but as medallions, and will receive about $3 profit per coin. The agencies will sell these coins regardless of the disruption in our system of coinage that may result.
I believe we were pushed into the Olympics. 1 am opposed to cities having any say about the Olympics in this day and age. We are not city states; we are nations. I have some knowledge of how the Olympics began. The cities of Carthage, Athens and Sparta competed against each other. Some of my colleagues may remember it, but I have no personal knowledge. These were city states. We no longer have city states. It is not to anyone's advantage to allow cities to hold the Olympics. Montreal is not alone; there are also the cases of Denver, Vancouver and Munich.
It is a fact that once the Olympics are awarded, they do not belong to the particular city but to the country. There is an obligation on the country to be responsible for them. Canada should be the most of the Olympics, not the city of Montreal. Representatives from Montreal see millions and millions of dollars being spent on a two-week show. That money should be spent on the development of parks, housing and sewage disposal. I question the priorities of some of the representatives of the city of Montreal.
Be that as it may, it is a fact that young people in every community from coast to coast are deprived of training facilities to prepare them to compete in international athletic competitions. They do not have a decent rink, pool, stadium or track. They do not have the elementary facilities for basic training which a nation as well off as Canada should expect of every community in this country. If we have this kind of money to spend, we should ensure that all communities have the facilities to develop amateur athletes.
We do not have an Olympic-size pool in northern Ontario. I remember a young fellow from Matheson. He learned to swim in the Black River, which is not very large. He did not have any professional training. He came third in at least two major events at the Canadian National Exhibition. Some of the best athletes in North America
July 25, 1973

competed in those events. He came from an earea which was not able to provide proper training facilities.
The town of Schumacher received the gift of a skating rink with artificial ice from McIntyre Mines long before most other communities had such a facility. We were able to train people like Barbara Ann Scott who went on to become the world figure skating champion. Most other figure skaters in North America trained in Schumacher, near Timmins: it was the only Olympic-size rink with full facilities which operated during the summer. We can expect great things from ordinary communities in Canada if we provide the basic requirements. If this government has the kind of money that is needed to provide a two-week international show, surely it should be able to help some of these communities.
I think the Olympics is all very nice; I sincerely believe that. However, I believe it will be a black mark against Canada if the people who compete in the Olympics are not provided with accommodation and the necessary facilities. This government should not have been tricked by Mr. Drapeau and Mr. Bourassa.
We should not have been tricked by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, in his overzealous assessment of the results of the last election, made it very clear that if the Olympics were to be held in Canada the taxpayers would not have to pay for it. We will have to pay for the Olympics. The Prime Minister will not be here, because the cost will not be known until 1978. Some of us will still be here. We will have to raise the money from the taxpayers to pay the debt incurred by the Olympics. I suggest it would be more honest for us to participate in the Olympics as a government. We should decide what the Olympics are to cost and put up the money.
It is unfortunate we do not have any say about where the Olympic events will be held. Some events should be held in Quebec City and Three Rivers. Kingston will be used to some extent. I do not think Ottawa and Toronto are too far away. Some of the events could be held in northern Quebec and northern Ontario. However, that could only come about if we were part of COJO, and we are not. I suggest that in the end we will have to put up the money.
Of all the hair-brained schemes Mayor Drapeau has dreamed up in the past, this one of selling the amount of currency he anticipates is probably the most unrealistic. If this were a medallion, I would not care.

If we are determined to put our currency in the form of collectors' items, the Mint must control its issue and make all decisions as to the quantity involved, and so on, as has been the case whenever commemorative coins have been minted in the past. The Olympic committee has pledged to this House that financing will be undertaken by them with the authority of this bill and they will not approach the federal government for any additional funds. As far as this party is concerned, we shall honour this commitment to the Canadian taxpayer. It was realized, however, that the study used the market distribution structure of the Munich games as its basis. The fact that Germany issued 90 per cent of its coins within its own boundaries, and the fact that only 25 per cent of the coins are to be issued on the Canadian market, could account for such a deficit prediction.
At the committee stage there was no evidence of any market research conducted into the coin and stamp proposals that would substantiate the government's proposed deficit.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) maintained that production would be regulated by market demand. In light of the lack of a market study, this appears to be a somewhat short-sighted reply or statement to the basis of the majority of the proposals which would supply the key financing for the Olympics. The original market distribution of coins announced by COJO was 35 per cent European and foreign, 25 per cent Canadian and 40 per cent United States. These figures, Mr. Speaker, if realized would account for COJO attaining its budget aims.
The proposed Post Office marketing board under the Postmaster General continues to be authorized to administer the promotion, distribution and merchandising of Olympic coins both within and outside of Canada. I sincerely trust, along with many Canadians, that the Post Office will be better able to distribute the coins than it has been able to distribute the mails.
To demonstrate some of the confusion and contradiction by the government on relevant issues of this bill one need only examine the proposal for a premium on the coins. The idea of a 10 per cent premium on the coins was first mentioned in committee by the Postmaster General. Later the same day the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) disputed this statement by saying that no premium was to be charged. These conflicting statements by two senior government members continue to illustrate that from the outset the government has been totally confused, ill-informed and ill-prepared in its dealings with the entire Olympic matter. We have once again, through the existence of an amendment, assured the Canadian taxpayer that no Olympic coins will be sold at less that face value.
The only people within the federal government who seem to have any knowledge whatsoever of what is taking place are the employees of the federal Mint who, I understand, had geared up for production of the coins even prior to second reading of this bill in the House. If the Prime Minister felt that passage of the bill was assured in its initial form, and on the strength of this he instructed the Mint to proceed with preparations of the coins, I can assure the hon. gentleman that he was most definitely mistaken, for without the amendments presently incorporated in this bill he would have had no such support from this House in so far as financing through the minting of these special coins is concerned.
Olympic Bill
The most effective way to assure sufficient sales is to adhere to the policy of limited mintage; in other words, a production and distribution ceiling. By promoting limited mintage the coin sales could be regulated and monitored to ensure that the market is available. The value of the coins would also be increased if limited mintage were practised. For example, the 1948 dollar, of which only 18,000 were minted, is now worth approximately $240.
In order to ensure that the Olympic organizing committee would receive its maximum expected revenue, our party took strong steps to add amendments to the bill which would place a $450 million production ceiling on the value of the coins issued. This was opposed by the NDP. This is more than enough to allow for a $260 million revenue to be obtained by COJO to satisfy their budget. To prevent a federal deficit which could result from overpayment, we initiated a $260 million revenue ceiling on moneys going to the Olympic organizing committee; $250 million from the sale of coins and $10 million from the sale of stamps.
The most important omission from the bill was the provision for an audit and general report to parliament. How this was omitted when Bill C-196 was first proposed is completely beyond any understanding. It continues to reflect the Prime Minister's attitude of not caring about this bill, save saying to the people of Quebec that he approved the legislation giving them authority to have their games. At the same time, he has offered no safeguards to the rest of Canada or to the taxpayer in general. The Progressive Conservative Party feels that safeguards are necessary and these safeguards must be explained to all Canadians so they will fully understand just how the Olympic financing is structured and how it will affect them.
The amendment insisted upon by this party is to allow for a biennial report from both the Postmaster General as well as the Minister of Finance, allowing parliament to retain strict control over its financial responsibilities to COJO. From these reports we will be able to gauge the market expectations for the coins and stamps and align production accordingly. Without such reports, as outlined in the initial bill, the Postmaster General would have had no real basis for calculation, nor could he ever expect to have had any basis for calculation. The same amendment provides the opportunity to bring this bill back into committee for any needed adjustments if and when necessary, this dependent upon the signature of 60 members requesting such action.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, of prime concern to this party was the likelihood that the coins would circulate, and had this in fact happened there were no contingency plans for the possible redemption of these coins. Therefore, we have now proposed an amendment, which has been accepted, to the legislation to control the circulation of this currency by giving the Minister of Finance the right to redeem coins at face value if, in his opinion, the amount of these coins in circulation would be detrimental to Canadian currency. The cost of redeeming the coins, minus the value of the silver content, will then be charged back to the Olympic account.
It was also feared, Mr. Speaker, that at some point in time these coins, being legal Canadian currency, would be

Olympic Bill
re-sold at less that face value. In order to ensure that the organizing committee and the federal government were not hindered in realizing their full expectations, the Progressive Conservative Party proposed an amendment to disallow the sale of these coins below face value. In this manner both parties should receive maximum value from the sale of each coin.
There is yet another point. The manufacture, distribution and sale of postal-related products could have had a damaging effect on the Canadian arts and crafts business, as these products were not adequately defined and the decision was left to the Postmaster General. There can be no question that the four year period from 1973 to 1976, inclusive, can provide an economic boom for Canadian crsftsmen from the sale of Olympic commemorative items to the tourist trade. If the postal-related products are not clearly defined, it can put the government in direct competition with private individuals who do not have the low overhead costs and the public funds of the Post Office Department. We strongly suggested that the bill be amended so as to discontinue this practice and to clearly define postal-related products. This has been done and the bill has been amended to cover this discrepancy.
We acknowledge that within the Canadian Olympic structure Montreal applied to become the host city for the 1976 games, and that it was a Canadian decision to nominate Montreal as the representative Canadian city for consideration as the host of the 1976 Olympics. The award went to Montreal on behalf of Canada, so let us not make any mistake or have any misunderstanding, some of which may have arisen because of the secretive way in which the Prime Minister has handled this matter from the outset. Had the Prime Minister been forthright in this respect to both the House and the Canadian people at the outset, this last minute panic, confusion and uncertainty would never have arisen.
In conclusion I reiterate, however, that we do not support the method in which this bill was presented to the House. The inexcusable delay in introducing this legislation serves only to illustrate the inaction and ineptness of the government. It is unfortunate that an event such as the 1976 Olympics, which can have such long-term advantages for the youth of Canada, the youth of the world and Canadians in general, should have been subjected to the secretive confusion surrounding the entire event. Nor will we relent in our questioning regarding the financing of the housing in the Olympic village where CMHC will be so heavily involved. To date, answers to questions regarding CMHC have been far from conclusive, have been far too general in scope and leave far too many questions unanswered in the minds of the members of this party.
Also, we should ensure that sufficient security is provided so that we do not have to concern ourselves with a repetition of the unfortunate incident at Munich. This matter also has been treated with vagueness and indifference by the Prime Minister and has resulted in questions being raised in the minds of of many Canadians as to what security in fact will be provided and at what cost to the Canadian taxpayers.

We shall continue our investigation into what appears to be a $25 million grant to the CBC to act as host televiser for the Olympic games. Unanswered questions in this area include, among others, why the CTV has continually offered its resources in the area of television and has not been asked to participate, thus greatly reducing the expenses of the CBC and ultimately the taxpayer. It is a known fact that CTV operates at a fraction of the cost of the CBC and provides a similar quality of coverage and commentary.
While the present administration has taken this matter lightly and has burdened private industry with its own responsibility, our party does not intend to sit idly by without closely scrutinizing the entire operation. It is with these amendments to the bill and with the points which I have mentioned in mind that the Progressive Conservative Party gives its support to Bill C-196 in its present form.

subtopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. LOUIS ST. LAURENT TRIBUTES TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. LOUIS ST. LAURENT TRIBUTES TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with profound sorrow that we have learned of the death of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. Canada has lost a great Canadian, but his work lives on and his name will always be associated with qualities that are respected and admired throughout the country.
The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, as a person, as a public servant and as a statesman, long ago won a permanent place in the affection and esteem of Canadians. His unfailing sense of courtesy and respect for others gave to him a quality of courtliness and kindliness which are encountered all too rarely today.
Mr. St. Laurent had a profound faith in Canada. He was motivated by a deep sense of public duty and believed there could be no greater honour than to serve one's country. He entered public life primarily to foster Canadian harmony. His contribution to the better understanding of Canada by Canadians was immense, and everywhere he became the symbol of tolerance and unity. His 16 years of public service were fruitful years for this country, domestically and internationally.
His legacy to Canada permeates Canadian life. As Minister of Justice, Secretary of State for External Affairs, and Prime Minister he played a leading role in the social, constitutional and judicial development of this country. He was, to use a phrase he once applied to others, an enlightened patriot. Canada is a better place because he lived among us.
I know that all Canadians join with me in expressing sympathy to Mr. St. Laurent's family.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. LOUIS ST. LAURENT TRIBUTES TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec and our country as a whole have lost a most distinguished citizen. His name was a symbol of the very strength of Quebec. As a Canadian citizen, father, lawyer and statesman, his life was an example of courage, determination and integrity. He was a great Quebecer, a great French-Canadian, in short, a great Canadian.
Passing of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent

Mr. St. Laurent achieved great respect in his profession as a member of the bar. His name was highly respected. When Mr. King called upon him to enter the government of Canada as minister of justice during the war, in the service of his country, Mr. St. Laurent was a great unifying force for Canada. He was a minister of extraordinary capacity and resourcefulness, as I was frequently told by one of his former distinguished colleagues, the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley.
It was not my privilege to serve with Mr. St. Laurent in the House of Commons. I observed him at a distance as a formidable, able party leader, a man who obviously inspired great public confidence. He was held in great respect throughout this country by those who served with him politically as well as by those who opposed him politically. He was regarded as a non-partisan leader. Although one may have differed with Mr. St. Laurent in opinion, one never questioned his sincerity or his intention to further the interests of his fellow citizens. He was regarded with great affection throughout this land.
I share the sorrow of the House in paying my respects at this time to the late Mr. St. Laurent, and I wish to extend my sympathy and the sympathy of the members of my party in this House to the members of his family.

subtopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. LOUIS ST. LAURENT TRIBUTES TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the death of any person, humble or great, is always a cause for sympathetic sorrow on the part of anyone with any sensitivity. But I think it is perhaps appropriate to say that one need not feel sorrow at the passing of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. Life is not eternal. It has to come to an end. And when it comes to an end at the age of 91 for a man who has given so much to society, and has won for himself so great a name in the history of his country, one can feel great joy in having been privileged to live in the same country with such a person.
I did not serve in parliament during Mr. St. Laurent's term in the various offices he held, but I did have the pleasure of meeting him on a number of occasions and of knowing him.
[ Transla tion]
I learnt that he was a very gentle, courteous and civilized man, Mr. Speaker, a man whose heart was one with that of the people of Canada. He understood the difficulties this country faces and with all his heart he wished for a united Canada. He was not only a politician, but the leader of a nation. He was not only the leader of his party, but the leader of the people of Canada as a whole.

Because he was such a person he won the respect of every Canadian. The great fact about a democratic system such as ours is that people differing in their politics or social philosophies have respect one for another.
On behalf of my colleagues and myself, I pay tribute to a man who won, and deserved, the respect of Canadians from coast to coast, who gave of himself unstintingly in the cause of Canadian unity and Canada's future. I join others in sending our sympathy to his family, in the knowledge that this man deserved to live and that Canada is the better for the fact that he lived so long and so well.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I are deeply moved by the sudden death of an illustrious son of Canada, and particularly of French Canada.
I had the good fortune to know the right hon. Louis St-Laurent when he was Minister of Justice and Secretary of State for External Affairs. I was a member of Parliament when he became Prime Minister, replacing the right hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
Often, in the evenings, when we were leaving Parliament, it happened that I left by the main door at the same time as Mr. and Mrs. St-Laurent. Having known him at a time when I was a relatively young member, I must say that I saw Mr. St-Laurent somewhat as a good Canadian family man, affable and not at all haughty. Everyone could talk to him. He was a true Canadian in the widest sense of the term, and I will never forget the role he played in keeping the various regions of Canada together.
Someone stated earlier that he was a great Quebeker, a great French-Canadian and a great Canadian, but I am sure that he was above all a true Canadian, a great French-Canadian, a man who was attached to his province, of course, but never to the detriment of anyone.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, we are so moved by his sudden death. May I, on behalf of my colleagues and myself, offer our most sincere condolences to Mr. St-Lau-rent's family.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. LOUIS ST. LAURENT TRIBUTES TO FORMER PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I speak with a heavy heart this afternoon. I knew Louis St-Laurent as a friend from the days when he was president of the Canadian Bar Association, one of the most distinguished lawyers of our country. I was a member of the council of the bar in those days, and the impression that he left with me in the early 1930s, when I got to know him well, has never been effaced with the passing years.
As has been said, he came into the House of Commons, I think it was in 1942. He had a call to come here to do his part to bring about a unity within this nation which at that time was deeply challenged. He gave up a tremendous law practice. I remember the first day that he spoke in this House as minister of justice. It was a lawyer's speech; it was a speech representing the epitome of the service that he was to render his country.
It is strange how our paths have crossed during the years. When he was minister of justice, I was opposition critic. He talked very freely with me at all times. I shall never forget the degree to which-I have spoken of this before-he made me the confidante of many of the things that he intended to do. Those things will not be written by me but they will always be a memory of one for whom I had not only respect but affection.
He became secretary of state for external affairs, and in large measure it was his concept that brought about the establishment of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. He became prime minister. Later, I became leader of the opposition in 1956, and the first message of good wishes that I received was from Louis St. Laurent.
Later I became Prime Minister and leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. I think of him not only as the great lawyer that he was but as a devoted servant of the Crown, for it was his invitation that brought about the visit of Her Majesty the Queen and the opening of parliament by the monarch for the first time in our history. He understood the meaning of justice and of equity. While reared in the province of Quebec with a knowledge of the Code, he had an abiding admiration for the common law.
It is difficult for me to speak of him in an impersonal sense. On occasion he would touch the heights in debate in this House. He and I were the last surviving members of Her Majesty's Imperial Privy Council in Canada. I do not speak of him with that admiration that I possess only now that he is gone. He knew it: he knew how I felt while he lived, and I never forgot his birthday, which was something that he very much appreciated.
A great Canadian in this place made his contribution to a united Canada, his life devoted to the establishment of one Canada, one nation, while at the same time maintaining, and rightly so, the traditional constitutional rights of his paternal ancestry. It is hard to speak of him as freely as I would like. He gave of his best and he loved his country. He never quite understood, despite his years at the bar, the clash of debate in the House of Commons. He represented the concept that, I am not ashamed to say in that I followed it through the years, realized that this institution is a place in which, as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said, we may disagree but we build up tremendous respect and regard for those who sit opposite.
I join in the expressions of deep mourning at his passing at a very advanced age, and in the sympathy extended to the members of his family. I couple with that my deepest appreciation that I was privileged to sit in this House for 15 years while he sat opposite. He loved Canada, he lived for Canada and his memory will be forever honoured in our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one will understand that being member for Quebec East and succeeding Mr. St-Laurent who had represented this constituency for 15 years, I wish to join my humble voice to that of the previous speakers and pay tribute to a great man who has just disappeared, the right hon. Louis St-Laurent.
I knew Louis St-Laurent quite well. For 15 years, I was not only closely involved in his political activities in the riding of Quebec East, but I had many opportunities of holding most interesting conversations with him. What always impressed me about this former Prime Minister of Canada is the dignity and composure of his conversations that made him so interesting as well as engaging.
In 1965, when it was a matter for me of being a candidate in the riding of Quebec East, I recall that the first person whom I visited and asked for advice was the right hon. Louis St-Laurent. And I still remember his words: Duquet, you have been in politics long enough and acquired a lot of experience; if you really want to be a candidate and become a federal member of Parliament in Ottawa, the only advice I can give you is to do it with the

July 25, 1973

same dignity as I myself tried to fulfill my mandate, always in a spirit of truth and in the specific purpose of trying to serve your fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, with such advice coming from such a man, it has been easy for me, for eight years, to fulfill my mandate and succeed the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent in the riding of Quebec East. The people of this constituency have maintained a sort of veneration for this great man and I am convinced that in the riding of Quebec East people are now crying because of the announcement of the death of Mr. St. Laurent, even though, due to his old age, we had to expect that.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute, like previous speakers, to Mr. Louis St. Laurent. To my mind, his death will leave quite a gap, not only in Canada, in this House and in the province of Quebec but everywhere he has been; it will stir deep emotion in all those who have known him; that is why I wanted to make a few modest remarks.
On behalf of the people of the riding of Quebec East, which I represent and which he so worthily represented from 1942 to 1957, I offer to the House of Commons, to the St. Laurent family, my very deepest and most sincere condolences.

Mr. Speaker, with consent, I would like to join all my colleagues and express my sorrow at the news of the passing away of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, as well as the pride I take in
Passing of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent
having learned much from him. He always struck me, as well in his behaviour as in his speech, as the very incarnation of the most noble values that distinguish the statesman.
For us, who endeavour to better serve our fellow citizens, we could find no better example of generosity, devotion to duty, wisdom and credibility.
In the story of his life, Canadians, the young ones in particular, will read whole chapters that will stir in them new faith in public men.
To the family of the illustrious deceased, I offer my heartfelt condolences.
